newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British unemployment at lowest since 1990.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British unemployment at lowest since 1990.

text.p: Unemployment in Britain fell by a better than expected 59,400 to 1.65 million in April, its lowest level since August 1990, official figures showed on Wednesday.

The unemployment rate fell to 5.9 percent in April from 6.1 percent in March in the 14th consecutive monthly decline. The jobless total was about 1.3 million down on its peak of near three million in 1992.

Britain's new Labour government, which had long accused the defeated Conservatives of concealing the true level of unemployment, immediately announced that the way the figures are calculated would be reviewed in an effort to make them more credible.
"Credibility must be restored to the official unemployment statistics," employment minister Andrew Smith said.
"I very much welcome, therefore, the opportunity to review this information through the announcement by the Office for National Statistics of a public consultation on the labour market statistics."
He added: "The public have suspected they have been the object of political manipulation."
Officials at the ONS said they would hold talks with economists, statisticians and the media about how best to present the figures. They hoped to bring in any changes by the late summer of this year.
Economists have criticised what they see as the low quality of Britain's current method of counting the unemployed.

Britain only includes those who are both out of work and claiming benefit. And over the past 18 years, the Conservative government, which was ousted on May 1, had tightened conditions for claiming that benefit.
The widely recognised International Labour Organisation measures unemployment as all those out of work and seeking jobs whether or not they can claim benefit.
Average earnings in March rose by 4.5 percent, unchanged from the previous month.
Both the unemployment and the average earnings figures were better than economic analysts had expected, although upward pressure on wages was seen increasing in the near future.
Peter Osler of brokerage GNI said: "Average earnings are a welcome surprise although the fall in unemployment is a little higher than we are looking for."
The London stock market remained firm but showed little reaction to the jobless figures. Sterling declined against the mark and the dollar.
